course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

topic.title: Sectional Conflict: Regional Differences
topic.summary: How immigration and nativism changed the North, how free labor and slave labor divided the economies of the two sections, and how abolitionists and defenders of slavery argued over slavery.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which two countries sent the largest numbers of immigrants to the United States in the 1840s and 1850s?
choices: Britain and France
Ireland and Germany
Italy and Russia
China and Japan
questions.explanation: Famine and economic hardship in Ireland and political and economic upheaval in Germany sent millions across the Atlantic.
choiceExplanations: Those countries sent immigrants, but fewer than Ireland and Germany.
Famine and economic hardship in Ireland and political and economic upheaval in Germany sent millions across the Atlantic.
Large migrations from those countries came later.
Chinese migration was smaller, and Japanese migration had barely begun.
questions.distinguisher: The Britain and France choice is close because those countries sent migrants for many years, but Ireland and Germany sent the largest numbers in these years.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a main cause of Irish migration to the United States in the late 1840s?
choices: A famine that followed the failure of the potato crop
The failure of the revolutions of 1848 in the lands of Europe
A British law that banned Irish farmers from owning any land in Ireland
An American program that paid Irish families to settle in the Midwest
questions.explanation: The potato blight that began in 1845 caused famine and death in Ireland, and many survivors left for the United States.
choiceExplanations: The potato blight that began in 1845 caused famine and death in Ireland, and many survivors left for the United States.
The revolutions of 1848 sent many Germans, not most of the Irish, to the United States.
Britain passed no such ban on Irish landowning.
No such program existed.
questions.distinguisher: The revolutions of 1848 choice is close because those events also drove migration, but they sent Germans to the United States, and the Irish left because of famine.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Many immigrants settled in ethnic communities in order to
choices: avoid the taxes that the government required of other residents of the cities
meet the legal requirements of the federal law that governed citizenship
preserve parts of their languages and customs and find support from neighbors
comply with state laws that kept immigrants apart from the rest of the population
questions.explanation: Ethnic neighborhoods gave newcomers churches, newspapers, schools, and neighbors who shared their language.
choiceExplanations: Immigrants paid the same taxes as other residents.
Federal law did not require ethnic neighborhoods.
Ethnic neighborhoods gave newcomers churches, newspapers, schools, and neighbors who shared their language.
No such laws required it.
questions.distinguisher: The tax choice is close because immigrants did face high costs of living, but they were not exempt from taxes.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The nativist movement of the 1850s was aimed mainly at limiting
choices: the spread of slavery into the western territories of the United States
the number of banks that could issue paper money in the Northern states
the right of women to speak at public meetings on reform and religion
the political power and cultural influence of Catholic immigrants
questions.explanation: Nativists feared that Catholic newcomers would be loyal to the pope and would change American politics and culture.
choiceExplanations: That was the aim of the free-soil movement.
The movement did not concern banking.
That was a different issue.
Nativists feared that Catholic newcomers would be loyal to the pope and would change American politics and culture.
questions.distinguisher: The spread of slavery choice is close because both movements shaped party politics in the 1850s, but nativists were concerned with immigrants.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helps to explain the rise of the Know-Nothing movement?
choices: Anger among Northern workers at the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
Fear that Catholic immigrants would be loyal to the pope and take jobs
A law that gave immigrants the right to vote after one year in the country
A ban on Catholic worship that Northern states had passed in the 1840s
questions.explanation: Many native-born Protestants feared the political and economic weight of the new Irish and German Catholic voters.
choiceExplanations: That anger helped the antislavery cause and not nativism.
Many native-born Protestants feared the political and economic weight of the new Irish and German Catholic voters.
Immigrants had to wait longer to vote.
No Northern state banned Catholic worship.
questions.distinguisher: The Fugitive Slave Act choice is close because the Act did upset Northerners in the same years, but it did not cause the nativist movement.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Free-soil Northerners argued that the expansion of slavery
choices: was a sin that had to end at once in every state of the Union
would lower the price of cotton and cause losses for Northern mills
violated the Fugitive Slave Act and the rights of the Northern states
would undermine free labor in the western territories
questions.explanation: Free-soilers feared that slave labor would crowd free workers out of the West.
choiceExplanations: That was the abolitionist argument.
Free-soilers did not make that argument.
The Act helped slaveholders and not free-soilers.
Free-soilers feared that slave labor would crowd free workers out of the West.
questions.distinguisher: The sin choice is close because many free-soilers did think that slavery was wrong, but their main argument concerned free labor and the territories.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between free-soilers and abolitionists?
choices: Free-soilers sought to end slavery everywhere, and abolitionists to stop its spread
Free-soilers were mostly Southerners, and abolitionists were mostly Northerners
Free-soilers sought to stop slavery's spread, and abolitionists to end it everywhere
Free-soilers favored violence, and abolitionists favored only voting
questions.explanation: Free-soilers wanted slavery kept out of the territories, and abolitionists demanded that it end throughout the nation.
choiceExplanations: The positions are reversed.
Free-soilers were Northerners.
Free-soilers wanted slavery kept out of the territories, and abolitionists demanded that it end throughout the nation.
Neither group was limited in that way.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed choice is close because it names the same two groups, but it gives each one the wrong goal.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a method used by abolitionists in the 1840s and 1850s?
choices: Helping people escape from slavery on the Underground Railroad
Passing laws in Southern legislatures to end slavery gradually
Calling a convention of the states to rewrite the Constitution
Taking control of Congress by winning a majority in every election
questions.explanation: Black and white abolitionists wrote, spoke, petitioned, and helped people escape, and some were willing to use violence.
choiceExplanations: Black and white abolitionists wrote, spoke, petitioned, and helped people escape, and some were willing to use violence.
Southern legislatures did not pass such laws.
No such convention was called.
Abolitionists were a minority.
questions.distinguisher: The legislatures choice is close because abolitionists did try to change laws, but they could not persuade Southern legislatures to end slavery.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Southern defenders of slavery claimed that it was a “positive good.” This claim is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A drop in cotton prices that had left slavery unprofitable in the South
Growing attacks on slavery by abolitionists and the profits that slavery produced
A Supreme Court decision that had ended slavery in the Southern states
A law that required the Southern states to compensate their slaveholders
questions.explanation: As abolitionists attacked slavery, Southern leaders moved from calling it a necessary evil to defending it as beneficial.
choiceExplanations: Cotton was highly profitable.
As abolitionists attacked slavery, Southern leaders moved from calling it a necessary evil to defending it as beneficial.
The Court issued no such decision.
Compensation to slaveholders was never required.
questions.distinguisher: The cotton prices choice is close because the economy shaped Southern arguments, but cotton was profitable, which gave slaveholders reason to defend slavery.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Lincoln most likely said that Republicans could “afford to let it alone where it is” in order to
choices: announce a plan to end slavery in the Southern states by act of Congress
argue that slavery was a good that should be expanded into the territories
ask Northern voters to give up the free-soil position in order to win the election
reassure listeners that Republicans would not interfere with slavery in the states
questions.explanation: Speaking in New York in 1860, Lincoln separated the Republican goal of stopping slavery's spread from any attack on slavery in the states.
choiceExplanations: He rejects interference in the states where slavery existed.
He opposes the spread of slavery.
He keeps the free-soil position.
Speaking in New York in 1860, Lincoln separated the Republican goal of stopping slavery's spread from any attack on slavery in the states.
questions.distinguisher: The plan to end slavery choice is close because Lincoln thought slavery was wrong, but the passage says that Republicans would leave it alone where it exists.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.5, KC-5.2.I.A and KC-5.2.I.C: Northerners who joined the free-soil movement portrayed the expansion of slavery as incompatible with free labor, while defenders of slavery called it a positive social good
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Abraham Lincoln, a Republican from Illinois who had not yet been nominated for president, in a speech to an audience of New York Republicans at Cooper Institute on February 27, 1860
stimulusBlocks.citation: Abraham Lincoln, Cooper Institute Speech (February 27, 1860), in Noted Speeches of Abraham Lincoln, Including the Lincoln-Douglas Debate. Project Gutenberg eBook #48364.
stimulusBlocks.note: In this part of the speech, Lincoln speaks to Southerners, and “they” and “their” refer to the defenders of slavery.
stimulusBlocks.text:
Holding, as they do, that slavery is morally right and socially elevating, they cannot cease to demand a full national recognition of it as a legal right and a social blessing.

Their thinking it right and our thinking it wrong is the precise fact upon which depends the whole controversy.

Wrong as we think slavery is, we can yet afford to let it alone where it is, because that much is due to the necessity arising from its actual presence in the nation; but can we, while our votes will prevent it, allow it to spread into the national Territories, and to overrun us here in these free States?

questions.subskillText: Explain the point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience of a source.

questions.prompt: According to Lincoln in the first paragraph, defenders of slavery in 1860 held that slavery was
choices: morally right and deserving of national recognition
a necessary evil that would end in time
a matter for each state and unconnected to the territories
an outdated system that the Constitution would soon end
questions.explanation: Lincoln describes defenders as “holding . . . that slavery is morally right and socially elevating,” and demanding “full national recognition” of it.
choiceExplanations: Lincoln describes defenders as “holding . . . that slavery is morally right and socially elevating,” and demanding “full national recognition” of it.
Lincoln says they now call it morally right.
He says they demand national recognition.
He does not say that they expected an end.
questions.distinguisher: The necessary evil choice is close because earlier Southern leaders held that view, but Lincoln says that defenders in 1860 called slavery right.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions about the sections is best supported by the second paragraph of the excerpt?
choices: Lincoln saw the dispute as a conflict over the tariff and federal spending
Lincoln saw the sections as agreed on slavery and divided on other questions
Lincoln saw the dispute as a conflict of belief over whether slavery was right
Lincoln saw the dispute as one that the South alone could end by changing its laws
questions.explanation: Lincoln says that “their thinking it right and our thinking it wrong is the precise fact upon which depends the whole controversy.”
choiceExplanations: The paragraph concerns slavery.
He says the sections disagree about slavery.
Lincoln says that “their thinking it right and our thinking it wrong is the precise fact upon which depends the whole controversy.”
He says each side thinks the other wrong.
questions.distinguisher: The tariff choice is close because economic issues divided the sections, but the paragraph names slavery as the whole controversy.
